Course Name: A historical perspective of Aerospace Engineering
Description: PART-I : Based on inputs from CLE (LASE program) Recommended Topics: -------------------- * The scientific revolution of the 17th century -- mechanics of the craftsmen and mathematics of the scholars are fused to explain the Universe.  * The 18th century enlightenment movement and growing dominance of the scientific worldview.  * The 19th century steam engine and electric generator, and the industrial revolution. Evolutionary perspectives in geology, biology and society. The professionalization of Science and development of its secular and elite character. * The 20th century - the birth of new physics and chemistry of the atomic and subatomic world, and related technologies. The birth of computing machines, aerodynamic and space technologies. The growing knowledge of cellular and molecular biology, and human diseases. * The 21st century - the global concerns for public health and pandemics, ecological devastation and agricultural crisis, social and economic inequality, remain and continue to grow.  PART-II : 1. History of Aerospace Engineering a. Aeronautics and Aerospace – Aircrafts and Rockets b. Basic structure/geometry/terminology of aircrafts and rockets c. Basic science of flight – Number of disciplines involved in aerospace technology d. Stories of flight – Across the world e. Evolution in flying – balloons and gliders f. Flight of heavier than air object – First flight, First rockets 2. Major milestones (discoveries and inventions) and its impact on society and industrial revolution, including negative impacts on the society. a. Global milestones – First balloon flight, powered flight, V2 rockets, Supersonic flight, civilian supersonic, Shuttle flights, SPACEX etc. b. Indian milestones – First Indigenous aircraft design- HF24, LCA, ALH, SLV, PSLV, GSLV etc. 3. Evolution of ethics and practices in the discipline – Nuclear and Chemical Weapons control, Export control laws etc. 4. Important persons, their biographies, struggle, and success. a. Indian and global 5. Voices from the field (invited talks from practitioners and professionals) – Have couple of talks every semester 6. Recent and cutting edge research in the discipline 7. Prospective directions of evolution of the discipline in the near future.

Content (List of the topics/sub-topics to be covered in the lectures/practicals/assignments): • Governing equations for compressible fluid flows – differential and integral forms, equation of states for perfect and real gasses, Reynolds and Favre averaging to deal with turbulent flow modelling. • Introduction to basics of hyperbolic partial differential equations - Characteristics, general solution and its application to linear hyperbolic system. • Properties of 1D and 2D Euler equations, elementary wave solutions, Riemann problem for Euler equations and its solutions. • Introduction to multi-dimensional finite volume method for Navier-Stokes equations – structured and unstructured grid formulations, cell centered and cell vertex approaches, static and moving grid formulations, evaluations of geometric quantities of control volume, data structures for unstructured grid computations, discretization of convective and viscous fluxes, temporal discretization, grid movement algorithms, stability conditions. • Development of upwind methods based on flux difference splitting – approximate Riemann solvers for 1D Euler equations, rotational invariance property and extension of Riemann solvers for 2D finite volume formulations, concept of genuinely multidimensional Riemann solver. • Higher order temporal and spatial discretizations in finite volume formulations; spurious oscillations, monotonicity, positivity, total variations diminishing, local extremum diminishing criteria, development of non-linear discretization techniques for non-oscillatory solutions. Description: Functions: Idea of functions using examples from Biology. E.g., concentration of proteins as a function of time. Periodic functions. Functions as graphs. Rate equations, Diffusion, Solving differential equations numerically.    Vectors and matrices, Coordinate systems: Scalars and vectors. Matrices. Descriptive statistics and Data display: Measurement scales. Continuous and discrete data; Summarizing data set: Histograms, Pie Charts, other ways of representing data. Distributions:  Quantities typically measured in experiments as random variables. Binomial distribution, Poisson distribution, Normal distribution, Exponential distribution, etc.    Basic idea of hypothesis testing: Basic introduction to z-test, t-test. Numerically computing z and t values (using software like excel).

1. Screening, enrichment, and isolation of microbes with a desired property. Representative examples of desired properties are (i) antibiotic resistance, (ii) production of industrially important enzymes such as proteases and lipases, (iii) degradation of specific environmental pollutants, (iv) heavy metal tolerance, (v) degradation and/or metabolism of food preservatives (e.g., sodium benzoate, etc.), etc. One or more of these properties (or any other topical property) can be chosen depending upon logistics (suitability and appropriateness of carrying out the experiment in the UG lab which is a BSL1 facility) and availability of resources such as human resources (expertise), ease of carrying out experiments at scale (cost of consumables vis-à-vis the number of students crediting the course), etc. 2. Characterization of the isolated microbe e.g., determining the resistance (antibiotics) or tolerance (heavy metal) profile, determination of MIC, etc. In case the property chosen is degradation of a chemical compound (e.g., an environmental pollutant), and if time permits, then one can attempt to elucidate degradation pathway and identify intermediates using chromatographic methods such as TLC, GC-MS, etc. 3. Growth properties and kinetics, calculation of doubling time and specific growth rate, enumeration of microorganisms using total viable count. 4. Purification of industrially important enzymes using conventional protein purification techniques such as ammonium sulphate precipitation, ion-exchange column chromatography, (hydrophobic column chromatography, gel-filtration column chromatography) and asses the yield and fold purification of the purified enzyme. 5. Phage isolation and characterisation and enumeration. Estimation phage growth parameters, one-step growth curve, phage-typing, phage specificity, etc. 6. Assessing the potability of water by enumerating the fecal and non-fecal coliforms, MPN, etc. 7. Immobilization of microbial cells by cell-entrapment method using agar, agarose or Ca-alginate and conduct fluidized bed reactor studies at lab scale for degradation of a chemical compound (e.g., an environmental pollutant).

Description: Course Objectives: To expose students to the history of civil engineering and role in building human civilisations. To expose students to the fundamentals of civil engineering relevant to challenges faced by society in the 21st century. To inspire students for leadership and excellence in their professional careers. To expose students regarding societal-scale and global challenges involving civil engineering domain with innovative, often multi-disciplinary, solutions. Learning Outcomes: An overall understanding of requirements of sustainable design of future infrastructure systems, particularly in the context of India’s rapid urbanization and growth. An ability to identify, formulate, and solve complex engineering problems by applying principles of engineering, science, and mathematics. Sensitivity towards challenges in infrastructure systems. An ability to apply engineering design to produce solutions that meet specified needs with consideration of public health, safety, and welfare, as well as global, cultural, social, environmental, and economic factors. An ability to function in a team and communicate effectively with a range of audiences (peers, PDFs, instructors). An ability to recognize ethical and professional responsibilities in engineering situations and make informed judgments, which must consider the impact of engineering solutions in global, economic, environmental, and societal contexts. Hands-on experience on design and implementation of innovative solutions including collection, analysis and interpretation of data, use of relevant state-of-art tools and engineering judgment to draw conclusions. Course Content: History, importance and success of Civil Engineering; Science & Engineering before medieval period; The scientific revolution of the 17th century -- mechanics of the craftsmen and mathematics of the scholars are fused to explain the Universe; The 18th century enlightenment movement and growing dominance of the scientific worldview. The 19th century steam engine and electric generator, and the industrial revolution. Evolutionary perspectives in geology, biology and society. The professionalization of Science and development of its secular and elite character; The 20th century - the birth of new physics and chemistry of the atomic and subatomic world, and related technologies. The birth of computing machines, aerodynamic and space technologies. The growing knowledge of cellular and molecular biology, and human diseases; The 21st century - the global concerns for public health and pandemics, ecological devastation and agricultural crisis, social and economic inequality, remain and continue to grow; Global urbanisation trends (Eg., ASCE Future Vision 2070, GIFT City, Amravathi, etc.); Planning process & their components (incl. problem identification); Future society requirements for sustainable growth – Rapid urbanisation, India’s urban future, Growth to ensure sustenance & sustainability; Societal, economic, developmental and technical considerations and their intersections; Infrastructure development; Identification of challenges – built environment, transportation, water/waste water and energy systems; Introduction to state-of-art tools for design of intelligent infrastructure; Prototyping and innovative solutions to the identified challenges; Group projects/Hackathons on select topics; Expert talks.

Description: Course Objectives: • To introduce students to the different types of data in civil engineering and how to process them. • To expose students to the fundamentals of learning from data relevant to civil engineering. • To inspire students to harness developments in artificial intelligence, machine learning and data science to understand and solve civil engineering problems. • To inspire students to implement data-driven modeling for infrastructure systems in a computer programming environment for futuristic civil engineering challenges. Learning Outcomes: • An overall understanding of data types relevant to civil engineering, particularly in the context of intelligent systems. • An ability to identify, formulate and solve complex civil engineering problems by applying principles of artificial intelligence, machine learning and data science. • An ability to implement data-driven modeling to address futuristic civil engineering challenges using a computer programming environment. • An ability to function in a team and communicate effectively with a range of audiences. • An ability to infer from data for knowledge enhancement, as well as civil engineering design, planning and management. • Hands-on experience on analysis and interpretation of civil engineering data, and use of relevant state-of-art machine learning tools to draw conclusions. Course Content: • Introduction to data-driven systems and examples from different fields of civil engineering, semantics and definitions of artificial intelligence and machine learning, different types and sources of data. • Introduction to linear models, simple and multiple linear regression, logistic regression, k-Nearest Neighbors approach. • Supervised Learning – Classification and Regression Part I: Decision trees and Support Vector Machines. Classification and Regression Trees (CART) – growing trees, pruning, variable importance measure, Bagging, Boosting and Random Forests; Support Vector Machines (SVM) - separating hyperplane, maximum margin classifier, support vector classifier, support vector machines. • Supervised Learning – Classification and Regression Part II: Artificial Neural Networks (ANN). Definition and types of neurons, neural network architecture, cost function, feed forward back propagation algorithm, multiclass classification, neural networks for regression, introduction to deep learning. • Unsupervised Learning Part I: Clustering. Definition of clustering, different distance measures, introduction to hierarchical and partitional clustering, k-means clustering, cluster validity indices, introduction to fuzzy logic and fuzzy c-means clustering. • Unsupervised Learning Part II: Multivariate Analysis and Dimension Reduction. Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Empirical Orthogonal Functions (EOF). • Group projects/research on select topics.

Description: Course Objectives: 1. To introduce the essence of the evolution of the Vernacular/Traditional building construction in human settlements. 2. To familiarize the students with the locally available construction materials and techniques. 3. To bring understanding of the sustainable shelter technology alternatives to the students and inspire them to adopt in their professional careers. 4. To sensitize students about the socio-economic context of shelter technologies and their role in the development of the country. Course Content: 36 Hours 1. Evolution of Traditional building systems and their role in Rural India (Present and in future) – Advantages for local economy, employment potential; Hurdles, people mindset, evolution, interventions required; Relationship among various trades, local livelihood, economy and sustainability in rural India – 2 hours 2. Construction Materials and Properties – Earth (Mud), Sun dried and Stabilised mud, Stones, Bamboo, timber, Lime, bricks, tiles, Agro based residues, use of edible items – 5 hours 3. Sustainable Walling and Foundation Alternatives, Sustainable Roofing Alternatives, Concrete Block Masonry, Structural design of masonry building (Low Strength masonry), Disaster resistant design and construction of load bearing masonry (IS 13828, NBC Part 6, IS 1893 and IS 4326) –Technologies: Bamboo Design and Construction (walling/frame/roof/floor), Reinforced Brick Panel Slab (CBRI) – 15 hours 4. Retrofitting and Repairs of Masonry Buildings for Vulnerability Reduction – Approach, procedure, details, cautions etc; Building code IS 13935 Seismic Evaluation, Repair, and Strengthening of Masonry Buildings – Guidelines, Case Studies – 5 hours 5. Sanitation alternatives – On site composting systems, Dry toilets, Low water consumption toilets, comparison of water born sewerage, Septic tank system; Appropriateness for different contexts – 2 hours 6. Sustainable Services – Off grid electricity, solar energy harnessing, Rain Water Harvesting, Solid Waste Management – 1 hour 7. Impact of Government policies on vernacular building systems – Kuchcha versus Pukka; Housing assistance programs (PMAY); Government infrastructure buildings; Post disaster rehabilitation programs; Promotion of Prefab shelters v/s People built shelters; Government policies on access to local materials – 2 hours 8. Long term Performance of different building systems –Quality issues, Aging, maintenance, vulnerability of all types of construction, Impact of elements and disasters; State of Building Artisans – Knowledge and skills – 2 hours. 9. Comparison of popular systems (vernacular v/s modern)– Costing, economics, carbon footprint, water footprint, execution, logistics, cultural heritage, identity of the area, centralized v/v decentralized. – 2 hours

This course will teach students how to think about problems in transport phenomena. Given a physical problem, students will learn how to formulate a consistent mathematical model based on first principles, and how to simplify and analyze the equations to obtain useful physical insights and make quantitative predictions. The scope of the course is limited to single-phase, laminar flows with transport of a scalar. However, we will consider nonlinear problems, including situation where fluid flow is coupled to heat/mass transport. Key Topics: Introduction and motivation - Continuum approach - Elementary kinematics - Reynolds Transport Theorem - Governing conservation equations - Cauchy stress tensor - Navier-Stokes equations - Brief history of the stress tensor and continuum mechanics - Non-dimensionalization and O(1) scaling - Perturbation methods - Domain perturbation - Singular perturbation - Illustrative problems - Thin gap flows - Taylor-Aris dispersion - Lyapunov Schmidt reduction – Instabilities. Illustrative problems: Electroosmotic flow in microchannels, Reaction in a porous catalyst, Pulsatile pipe flow, Curved channel Dean flow, Wavy-wall flow, Settling sphere, Active flow in the cell cortex, etc.

Description: In this course, we will explore the latest research on identifying and countering these threats, covering topics such as systems for firewall detection and circumvention, web tracking and traffic analysis countermeasures, anonymous communication networks like Tor, and other privacy-enhancing technologies (PETS). * Traffic filtering: Introduction : what is traffic, how it is different from standard firewall operations, different levels in different ISPs? * Traffic filtering triggers : What type of content is filtered? Technical mechanisms to identify what type of content blocking. This involves studying IP tables, constructing packets using Raw Sockets to bypass protocol stack in the kernel etc. * Measurement Techniques to detect firewalls : How to assess blocking, different detection approaches with limitations etc. Studying SSL and TLS protocols in detail, identifying information leak in DNS, HTTP and TLS protocol. Use of traceroutes to learn about the network paths, identifying the network hop of the firewall etc. * Great Firewall of China (GFC) : One of the most sophisticated content blocking apparatus deployed at the country scale. Studying how network security researchers remotely characterize the filtering capability of the GFW for more than two decades. This involves studying creation of Transmission Control Block (TCB), how custom packets can break the TCB etc. * Identifying loopholes in firewalls : Characterizing sophisticated middleboxes (modified firewalls) deployed by different ISPs, measuring end-to-end delays using HTTP Ping, Iperf etc., caused by these middleboxes * Privacy: Overview : Different definitions and expectations of privacy; notions of Privacy at different network layers * Privacy: Web tracking: How a user is tracked over the web; tracking cookies; browser fingerprinting etc. Can firewalls help in user tracking? * Privacy: Anti-tracking techniques: Tracker list, ad-blockers, cookie partitioning etc * Privacy: Privacy Law: High-level idea of GDPR, CCPA and DPDPA etc., and detailed know how of their technical implementation * Privacy: Anonymity over Internet: Definitions of anonymity, why anonymity etc * Privacy: Anonymity Solutions: Proxies, Tor, Mixnets (intro) Course Modalities: Combination of in-class lectures, paper reading, hands-on components--programming assignments, projects.

Description: Progress in machine learning is often measured under controlled, well-understood conditions. However, safety-critical workflows in realistic settings require ML systems to be reliable even when faced with new and unexpected conditions. Sufficiently adverse conditions may violate the statistical assumptions underlying common ML models, causing undesirable behavior. This undesirable behavior may manifest in different ways such as: i) lack of robustness to unseen and adversarial inputs, ii) leakage of private data or model parameters, and iii) uneven performance across data partitions. This course will equip students to i) on the theoretical front, rigorously reason about conditions under which unreliable behavior occurs and ii) on the practical side, use these insights to build robust ML systems.Part 0: Recap of supervised and unsupervised learningPart 1: Robustness to out-of-distribution, noisy and adversarial data- Distribution drift, anomaly, and out-of-distribution sample detection; sample noise, label noise (Tsybakov and Massart); dirty-label poisoning attacks, clean-label poisoning attacks, bilevel optimization for poisoned data construction; limits of learnability and robust model design for poisoning attacks; white-box evasion attacks, query optimization for black-box evasion attacks, jailbreaking of foundation models; lower bounds on test-time robustness via optimal transport;generalization bounds for adversarial learning; training of (verifiably) adversarially robust models.Part 2: Data and model privacy- Linkage, membership inference, data reconstruction and website fingerprinting attacks; privacy definitions, differential privacy; differentially private learning (DPSGD and variants), privacy-utility trade-offs; privacy and convergence in distributed and decentralized learning; cryptographic protocols for private learning including multi-party computation; robustness-privacy tradeoffs arising from Byzantine and model poisoning attacks.Part 3: Transparency and explainability- Data partition bias in models, bias amplification, data auditing; interpreting outputs of complex models, fragility and impossibility of interpretability, interpretable model building; introduction to causal inference; explainable learning through the lens of causality; adversarial machine learning as a tool for restoring user agency; multi-objective optimization to investigate robustness, privacy, bias, and utility trade-offs.

Description: Many modern machine learning applications rely on data collected by the edge-devices. However, collecting this data at a central location (often called server) is often infeasible (due to the underlying high communication cost) or undesirable (due to privacy concerns). The energy industry is seeing an influx of data from new ICT and IOT interventions, leading to several problem statements seeking data-driven solutions. The problems span a wide gamut - from forecasting to pattern recognition, from anomaly detection to predictive maintenance and from cost minimization to efficiency optimization to name a few. This course can provide an introductory platform to the evolving world of energy informatics to interested students. Moreover, this course is ideally suited to introduce project/activity-based learning in the Electrical Engineering curriculum. It is an excellent sequel to the newly introduced AI and data science course EE 353, allowing students to apply the techniques learnt in that course to industry inspired problems. The course will also bring in industry professionals to provide insights on real world problems and also to evaluate the innovative solutions designed during the course. This way, the course is designed to produce well rounded energy data analysts much needed today. Module 1 (Introduction to energy data analytics and energy systems):Introduction to energy data analytics, focusing on the importance of data in theenergy sector. Overview of the key sources of energy data (smart meters,sensors, satellite data, etc.) and the typical tools and programming languages(Python, R, SQL, etc.) used for energy data analytics. Brief overview of energysystems, including generation, transmission, and distribution networks;renewable/conventional energy sources; consumption patterns and gridoperations.Module 2 (Data Processing and Exploratory Analysis): Data acquisition fromIoT devices, SCADA, and APIs. Data cleaning and preprocessing techniques(handling missing values and outliers). Time series analysis in energy data.Correlation between different energy variables. Pattern identification andanomaly detection. Typical machine learning applications in energy domain(demand forecasting, anomaly detection, consumer clustering, etc).Module 3 (Overview of various data-driven applications in energy domain):Forecasting energy demand and supply using time series techniques (ARIMA,SARIMA, LSTMs); Impact of weather on energy demand; Considerations inlong-term/medium-term/short-term forecasting.Optimization and decision support systems for energy efficiency optimization,demand-side management, building automation and control, energy costminimization and system control.Use of data for energy market analysis and policy studies, including electricitypricing models, carbon footprint analysis, energy transition studies.Overview of phasor measurement units and wide-area monitoring and control forpower grids.Role of IoT in smart energy systems (buildings cities, grids etc), big datatechniques for handling large-scale energy datasets, Cloud and edge computingapplications.Case studies and industry applications (examples include energy theft detection,power purchase cost optimization, power management in data centers)

Course Name: Advanced Integrated Circuits for Wireless Transceivers
Description: A traditional first course on Radio Frequency (RF) Integrated Circuit (IC) course (EE619: RF Microelectronics Chip Design) covers foundational RF concepts and the design of basic RF building blocks. This advanced course will build on these foundations and familiarize students with the design principles and practices of modern 5G wireless communication transceivers implemented in fully integrated form in nanoscale CMOS technology. A major part of the course will cover the fundamentals of multi-antenna transceiver design commonly employed at mm-wave frequencies (>30 GHz), where the design of phased-array systems and their constituent building blocks will be covered.   Part I (Foundations – 35% of the lectures): • Si-based devices in SiGe/CMOS: transistor modeling, process characterization, gm/Id design methodology. • Si-based passives in nanoscale CMOS: inductors, capacitors, transformers, transmission lines (TL), impact of BEOL and modeling. • Review of RF impairments of noise/distortion, TL, and S-parameters. • Two-port network theory, and application to microwave/mm-wave amplifier design (stability and noise of two-ports, amplifier noise/noise parameters/noise circles, power gain/ gain circles /stability circles etc.). • Review of complex baseband (I/Q signal processing), and modern RF architectures to enable image rejection, advanced filtering etc. Part II (mm-wave IC design – 65% of the lectures): This part of the course will build on the concepts developed in Part I and cover the fundamentals of multi-antenna transceiver design at mm-wave frequencies. Topics that will be covered include: • Introduction to phased arrays and multi-antenna systems. • System-level link-budget analysis. • mmWave amplifier design: low-noise amplifiers. • Phased-array transceiver building blocks: phase-shifters/vector-modulators, quadrature hybrids, coupled-resonators, variable-gain amplifiers, and couplers/power-dividers. • mmWave VCOs. • mmWave power-amplifier design. • Case-studies of state-of-the-art mm-wave transceivers. Students will be assigned a multi-stage design project, featuring a study of system requirements and translation to circuit design specifications, followed by hand-analysis/behavioural-modelling, transistor-level circuit design, layout design and characterization electromagnetic structures, and finally post-layout characterization.

Description: This course offers an introduction to the 1) impact of AI on startups and businesses, and 2) the emergence of new AI startups. Students will learn how AI is useful for businesses, and analyse the kind of functions and areas where AI may be applied. Students will learn how AI driven data feed into decision-making and more efficient processes. The course will also discuss how to think about the impact of AI implementation, and what leadership means in a rapidly changing AI-driven scenario. Students will learn about the pitfalls of AI including working with low-quality data, and ethical implications of Gen AI. In this course we will cover the following aspects: 1. Introduction to Gen AI and the AI landscape and why it is important for businesses to look at and understand AI. 2. Examples and use cases of how AI is applied in different business functions and sectors. How AI tools can be used in common business domains, functions and processes, how AI-driven data feeds into decision-making. We look at AI implementation examples in different business functions. 3. New business opportunities emerging out of AI and emerging AI first business. 4. Impact of AI on industries and sectors 5. Responsible AI: Ethics, Bias, Regulation 6. Role of leadership and change management: how to lead and manage AI-driven change.

Description: FinTech is transforming how we access, use, and think about financial services. From digital payments and lending platforms to AI-driven investment tools and blockchain innovations, technology is creating new possibilities for disruption across the financial sector.This course offers a practical and accessible introduction to the world of FinTech, ideal for aspiring entrepreneurs, professionals, and curious learners alike. Course Name: Advanced topics in deep learning for image analysis
Description: The course will deal with advanced deep learning techniques used to solve critical inference problems in remote sensing, image analysis, and computer vision. We plan to cover the following learning paradigms which consider learning a classification model under different levels of supervision. Meta- learning and few-shot learning Zero-shot learning Self-supervised learning Multi-modal learning Multi-task learning Continual learning Domain adaptation and generalization Uncertainty estimation in deep learning We will consider the application of the aforementioned learning algorithms for visual inference tasks with focus to image classification and semantic segmentation. To this end, land-cover classification from remote sensing images of varied modalities would be the running application example that will be discussed at length for all the algorithms. In addition, we will consider a few challenging classification problems in remote sensing (cross-sensor data retrieval, change detection, and land cover map generation for geographically disjoint and large areas) and show how some of these learning techniques (domain adaptation, uncertainty estimate) can be modified to solve these problems. Finally, annotation is a major problem in remote sensing, we plan to discuss how off-the-shelves self-supervision can be used as an alternative in this regard. Like the examples from the remote sensing area, we will consider examples from natural image and video analysis literature concerning very large-scale datasets (ImageNet, DomainNet, to name a few).

Academic English refers to the specific language skills required for success in academic or educational contexts, particularly in higher education. It encompasses the language skills necessary for reading academic texts, understanding lectures and presentations, engaging in academic discussions, writing summaries, and participating in other academic activities. The goal of this course is to measurably build on students’ academic English language skills by engaging them in listening, speaking, reading, writing, and grammar learning activities that are relevant to their academic life at the Institute as appropriate to the levels. Course Objectives Listening 1. Use listening strategies such as prediction, identification of main ideas and supporting details. 2. Respond appropriately to spoken instructions. 3. Recognize spoken language contexts and the appropriate variety of spoken English. 4. Identify phonetic properties of spoken English to help with accent correction Speaking 1. Speak with increased accuracy and fluency using basic and moderately complex sentences. 2. Verbally connect ideas in a discourse or conversation and paraphrase texts. 3. Use appropriate intonation and speech rhythms. 4. Express personal opinions with supporting information. 5. Make formal and informal oral presentations. Reading 1. Read and comprehend texts of increasing complexity. 2. Use reading strategies such as scanning, annotating, predicting, inferring, and identifying main ideas and other supporting information in the text. 3. Use strategies to recover the meaning of unfamiliar words from context. 4. Improve reading rate appropriate to the level. 5. Understand the writer’s intent and voice. Writing and Grammar 1. Demonstrate an understanding and application of grammar rules appropriate to the level 2. Apply punctuation correctly. 3. Compose simple, complex, compound sentences. 4. Use structural conventions to compose paragraphs. 5. Practice basic self- and peer-editing skills Across Domains 1. Be able to acquire and use new words and phrases. 2. Understand the inconsistent relationship between pronunciation and English spelling. 3. Demonstrate understanding of grammar in speaking and writing. 4. Create moderately complex sentences with basic transitions to connect ideas in speech and writing. 5. Identify patterns including event sequences, causes and effects/outcomes, comparisons and contrasts, and so on.

Course Name: Archives and Museums as sites of Historical Inquiry
Description: Archives and Museums are powerful cultural institutions worldwide. They serve as spaces where the state, scholars, and the public interact with diverse traces of the past, and interpret and narrate histories. While these two institutions share similarities,they also differ in significant ways, yet both playing a crucial rolein preserving and disseminating hete rogenous knowledge of the past. The course will explore archives and museums through global examples, examining their histories, structures, and their contemporary relevance. It will offer a critical lens on how the yshape our perception of past, history and collective memory.The course is organized around the following key themes/modules:1. What is Museum? Understanding different types of museums, the field of museology, and the history of museums, with a particular focus on South Asia from the colonial era to the present.2. Life of a museum: Exploring the processes of Collection,Documentation, Preservation, Curation, and Exhibition3. Visiting a museum: Analyzing the Politics of Curation,the dynamics of heterogenous Gaze and the Interpretation of the exhibits.archives and Vernacular Archives, as well as their Working, Organization and Management.5. Reading the Archive: Examining Archives as sites of power, tools for both Recovering and Erasing history, and their intersection with issues such as gender, sexuality and the environment etc.6. Between Paper and Artifact: The concluding module will explore the similarities, differences and intersections between museological and archival practices and perspectives.

Course objective: The understanding of human physiological and psychological functions is one of the most useful and beneficial assets in a technological and industrial environment. It is for better management of human life that one must have a good understanding of human behaviour, thoughts and feelings. Among these, stress is one of the most common psycho-physiological phenomena of today and moreover, the young have been found to be its usual victims. In fact, stress and its emotional components result from the complex interaction of genetic, physiological, behavioural, and environmental factors, which finally disturb the homeostasis (balance among internal physiological conditions) of the body. This course is designed to cover the entire field of enquiry as given above. Course outline: Fundamentals of behavioural health. Behavioural health and industrial hazards, health aspects related to personality (focus on Type-A personality pattern, converted Type-A persons who are a great challenge of the 21st century), perception and emotionality. Drug addiction and rehabilitation. Alcoholism and other substance abuse. Understanding stress and its various causes. Stress and psychologically-oriented and physically-manifested disorders [Psychosomatic disorders] Manic depressive tendencies, socialization problems, eating disorders. Depression and other related psychological states that are also manifest in the technological/industrial environment. Stress and adjustment :Occupational, social, marital, sexual and environmental aspects. Technology and subjective well-being (SWB)

Course Name: Things that Remain: Understanding the Past through Objects
Description: We are surrounded by objects. Objects tell much about who we are and shape our life in myriad ways. Often what survives from the past is only their material traces. This course focuses on a range of objects to explore the ways in which they can help us understand the past. It encourages the student to observe closely and analyse the familiar, in new ways. With tangible objects as the entry point, the course introduces the students to important approaches and concepts in the fields of archaeology, material histories and museum studies. The course will use diverse examples drawn from around the globe to familiarize the students with these Key modules in the course include 1. Module 1: Understanding Material Culture-This module looks at the complex and evolving relationship between people and the objects they create, live with, and produce. Starting from the pervasive presence of objects in our daily life, it will open up a discussion on how objects functioned in the past. 2. Module 2: Physical Remains of the past-This module will introduce the different types of physical remains of the past that archaeologists, and historians study. These range from every day objects such as pottery to artistic creations and architectural remains. Module 3: Archaeology as the study of Material Culture This module will focus specifically on archaeological approaches to the study of objects. It will address the basics of how archaeologists encounter, document and interpret objects. Module 4:Apporaches to Object Pasts-This module will look at the varying approaches that researchers employ to understand objects as integral to past lives. How do researchers study material remains to understand past lives such as everyday, social organization and social practices. The module will discuss approaches such as object biographies, Chaîne opératoire, and object itineraries Module 5: Displaying Objects-Past and present are integrally related and this relation is often reflected in our modern practices related to material remains. This module will look at practices of displaying material objects such as collections, exhibitions and museums

Course Name: History as a Discipline: Elementary Concepts
Description: This course intends to introduce history as a discipline to undergraduate students. While students have read the histories of particular places, times and objects at school (and thus history is not a new subject), they will benefit by learning the ideational processes whereby the study of history got instituted as a compulsory component of school-level education across the world since the nineteenth century. The course is thus a history of ideas that have had a global currency in modern times. Specifically, it delves into the history of the institutionalization of the modern discipline of history. It will probe into why the nineteenth and twentieth century world has often been described as the most historically minded of all ages. In doing so, the course will draw out the differences between the ‘post-Renaissance sense of the past’ and older conceptions of history (the history of Herodotus, Thucydides, for example, or the itihasa-purana traditions of India). A part of the course will, in fact, explore in depth these older traditions. The focus will be on early Indian traditions of engaging with the past—the many facets of itihasa in the long history of the Indian subcontinent. Literary traditions in India go back to more than two millennia: royal biographies, inscriptions, genealogies, chronicles.Thus, the subcontinent had produced numerous texts of recognizable historical intent and value. The term itihasa-purana, referring to that which was believed to have happened in the past,is mentioned in Vedic literature from early to mid-first millennium BC. Itihasa, itivritta, gatha, purana, akhyayika, udaharana, carita, vamsavali, etc. find place of prominence in Brahmanic, Buddhist and Jaina traditions. Jinasena, the ninth century Jaina author of the Adipurana, defines itihasa as relating that which actually happened. There were also changes in the genre of texts associated with itihasa. Besides the itihasa purana traditions, there were the Sramanic and bardic traditions of historical engagement in early India. Comparing with these diverse traditions of historical thinking, the course will familiarize students with how, with the onset of modernity, a rupture was brought about in the dominant definition of history and historical consciousness. This was also the time that history as a formal course of study was introduced into universities (that is, as part of school and college education). A separation was now fastidiously drawn between myth and history; between the supernatural and the natural; and between natural history and human history. As per this distinction, human history was to do only with events consciously actuated and influenced by human-beings. The course has two broad focus areas. One is the process of historical knowledge formation: how the practitioners of the discipline of history reconstruct the past. The other is the exploration of the shifts and turns in the debates on the relation between the natural sciences on the one hand, and humanities and history on the other. The philosophers of the Enlightenment conceived of history as a science—the science of evolution of society. They believed in the ideal of a unified system of all sciences, natural and humane. Another strain of thought, which became predominant in the field of history from the late nineteenth-early-twentieth century, effected a fundamental chasm between human history and the natural sciences. The ‘man-made’ came to be understood as distinctly different from the ‘natural’. The former demanded understanding from the historian, who was supposed to have an inside-view of the matter by entering the minds of the historical actors, while the latter, it was assumed, could be studied only through external observation. beings.The course has two broad focus areas. In the era of Anthropogenic climate change, this distinction gets obfuscated as human action has impacted the biosphere. History thus faces a novel task: its tradition of resolving questions of justice and morality and capacity for empathetic understanding have perhaps to be extended to the entire world of natural reproductive life. The course will benefit students by laying out some basic lines of convergences, unities and tensions between the sciences and the humanities, on the one hand, and between diverse pre-modern/ non-modern sensibilities about the past and a hegemonic modern sensibility, on the other. Content: 1. Unit 1: Pre-modern traditions of engaging with the past. We will focus on the many facets of the itihasa purana traditions in the Indian subcontinent. (See elaboration in the above section.) The module will explore the forms and contents of these genres. 2. Unit 2: The global discourse around history since the nineteenth century. In an era of unprecedented, rapid and dramatic historical transformation that characterized the world since the onset of the Industrial Revolution, history could no longer be simply the model or precedent for the present, as it sometimes functioned before. In this unit, we study the concept of scientific history in the nineteenth century which saw history as laying bare the direction, mechanism and laws of human evolution. Generalized patterns of rise and fall, growth and decay, progress and decline of civilizations; of the evolution of governments and governance, of economic development, etc. were sought to be mapped in the same manner in which geological and biological evolution were being researched. In this unit, we study the concept of empiricism in history—how the supposed assumptions of science were transferred to the social sciences. 3. Unit 2: The historian’s craft—on how methods of writing the past evolved through the turn of the centuries; the processes of condensation, realignment and selection in the reconstruction of the past; the relations between the present and the past; the historian and his facts; the nature of historical evidence, etc. The Collingwoodian concept of the historian as ‘actor’ and not just ‘spectator’—‘entering the minds of another’; imaginative understanding versus explanation; the problem of historical interpretation. 4. Unit 3: “Two cultures”? History and Science—the many debates across the last three centuries over the relations between the study of human history and the study of nature.between the study of human history and the study of nature. 5. Unit 4: Rethinking History in the time of anthropogenic climate change. Certain fundamental ideas about what human-beings can cause/ make or cannot cause/ make have undergone radical revision in the era of global warming.The geophysical agency of human beings is an unprecedented concept. Human history is thus getting re-conceptualized at present. This module focuses of this current rethinking of history. The history of modernity becomes the history of human ecological overreach by grave proportions. The certitudes of human history—of progress, technological mastery over nature, etc.—get unsettled when juxtaposed against the history of natural life on the planet.

Description: Our access to our city is mediated by technologies, systems, conventions and most of all, by our embodied limits. This course proposes to introduce the city as our prime repository of design problems. Its purpose is to introduce students to ways in which they can begin to understand urban problems. The city offers problems which are at once of a social and technical nature, and introducing students to this area of interdisciplinary scholarship will be helpful to them in developing their own future work.This course introduces students to the city through lectures, films and assignments. Students will learn to inquire into the city around them and the many systems which constitute it as a social and physical environment. Assignments and projects will involve field work and class work to describe, diagnose and propose interventions at a human scale.At the end of this course, students will be have learnt (a) to read the city in terms of the many systems which co-exist within it, (b) techniques of mapping urban phenomena, and (c) several theoretical and conceptual perspectives from which the city has been examined in the interdisciplinary literature

Contents This is an introductory course on the design process of interactive products. The course will introduce user centred design methods such as contextual inquiry, analysing interviews, affinity diagrams, personas, scenarios, prototyping, and design evaluation. The course will also introduce some theoretical elements of human-computer interaction (HCI) such as the layers of user experience, modelling users with stages of use models, conceptual models and heuristics and principles of good interaction design. If time permits, the course may cover some related topics such as interaction techniques, usable security, user experience metrics, integrating HCI in software development and the history of HCI. Through the course, the students will get an opportunity to apply their learnings in a course project in which they will design an interactive product. Depending on the interest of the students, the product may either be a website, a mobile app or a hardware product. In this project, the students are expected to do fieldwork to identify problems, propose alternative designs, prototype one of them and evaluate it.

 The scientific revolution of the 17th century -- mechanics of the craftsmen and mathematics of the scholars are fused to explain the Universe.  The 18th century enlightenment movement and growing dominance of the scientific worldview.  The 19th century steam engine and electric generator, and the industrial revolution. Evolutionary perspectives in geology, biology and society. The professionalization of Science and development of its secular and elite character. The 20th century - the birth of new physics and chemistry of the atomic and subatomic world, and related technologies. The birth of computing machines, aerodynamic and space technologies. The growing knowledge of cellular and molecular biology, and human diseases. The 21st century - the global concerns for public health and pandemics, ecological devastation and agricultural crisis, social and economic inequality, remain and continue to grow.  Overview of Thermal engineering: The thermal and fluids engineering stream deals with processes that deal with transfer of energy and motion of fluids, in both coupled and uncoupled manner. Since a significant section of mechanical engineering deals with generation of power, and almost the entirety of this power is generated by means of techniques that deal with transferring energy from some form to another form, thermal and fluids engineering plays a significant role. Besides the generation of power, most systems from mechanical engineering have to deal with either absorption or dissipation of heat, and with some or other form of fluids. Hence, the principles learnt in this stream are useful throughout the entire domain of mechanical engineering. Overview of Design engineering: The design stream deals with the conceptualization of the machine that needs to be produced. The process begins with a thorough assessment of the need of such a machine. Once the necessities are clearly ascertained, the design process in initiated involving various methodologies of analysis, such as stress analysis, thermal analysis, analysis of the kinematics and dynamics of the machine including the transfer of motion and power, an analysis of manufacturability, etc. The analysis is conducted on both the machine as a composite unit as well as its components. Finally, the drawings of the manufacturable design are created and passed on to the engineers specializing in the manufacturing stream. Overview of Manufacturing engineering: The manufacturing stream is involved with the manufacturing of components for the machines that were designed by the engineers specializing in the design stream. The process begins with identification of the proper raw materials, moves on to the choice of the machines that would be utilized for machining the components, and finally the machining process itself with its associated controls over dimensions and tolerances. Engineers in this stream are constantly attempting to innovate methodologies that allow production of the machines and their components with the best of quality, but with also with least amounts of debris and the least possible cost.

The course is designed for students who are interested in understanding entrepreneurship, forming companies, affecting social impact through entrepreneurship, corporate innovation, or investing in startup ventures. Even if the student is not interested in starting a venture of their own, understanding the entrepreneurial process will enhance productivity even in large organizations. a) Students will learn an entrepreneurial framework by which to workshop an original idea, culminating in a 2-minute video elevator pitch competition. Student also will be given to understand the existing entrepreneurial ecosystem available in IITB-SINE. b) Students will practice evaluating other ideas by rating/judging peer 2-minute video pitches, and then teams will be formed around the best ideas. In addition, student teams will meet to prepare for their visit to the U.S. and to prepare for the June assignments (case studies and final pitch competition). c) Students will visit the St. Louis entrepreneurial ecosystem, meet with U.S. entrepreneurs and investors, engage in case study discussions, and compete in a final team-based pitch competition. d) Students who complete the course will have a thorough understanding of the various facets of entrepreneurship and the mindset of an entrepreneur; will refine their language and understanding of entrepreneurship; will understand how to evaluate new business opportunities; will learn how entrepreneurship incorporates and integrates other business disciplines in the development, management, and exit of a start-up venture; will understand how entrepreneurial principles might be used in other organizations; will understand the risks and rewards of pursuing opportunities in entrepreneurship and will be able to knowledgeably evaluate whether or not entrepreneurship may be a career interest. Description: NOTE: The concepts introduced in this course (in comparison to the existing Consumer Behaviour course) have been highlighted in italics. Deformation response of materials at elevated temperatures: creep curve, creep mechanisms, deformation mechanism maps.

Description: PS 643-Introduction to AI, Data, and Policy is one of the two new courses, one introductory PS643 and one advanced PS 644 which replaces the old course PS 626-AI, Data and Policy which has been running for four years as an institute elective. PS 644 offered in Spring will have PS 643 as a prerequisite. While PS626 was only available to grad students, PS643 is also open to final year undergrads.   This course is an interdisciplinary introductory course for AI and policy. It will bring the student up to scratch with the landscape of extant policymaking on AI as well as make certain they learn the basic concepts, digital and philosophical, of AI, machine learning, and data, learn to code a small AI artefact, learn about basic AI and data policy and governance structures as they exist in India and worldwide, and the ongoing debates on the same. By the end of the course, the student would have learnt a basic amount of what AI technologies are, how data interacts with them, how they influence and are influenced by the world, and how to design policy around them. Students with a background in technology but wishing to learn the social impact of AI, or conversely with a background in the social sciences wishing to understand the technology of AI, will be benefited from this course. There are no prerequisites to this course but there are expectations the student will learn. Topics to be covered: • Basic ML, NLP, and CV • AI, its History, and Concepts • Extant AI and Data Governance • Fairness, Accountability, Transparency, Ethics, Human Rights • Indian AI Policy • Data Regulation, EU and India • AI and Surveillance

Description: The increasing mobility of people and goods across different geographical scales is an important aspect of the interconnected contemporary world. Many experts and policy makers view this as desirable, or at least inevitable, while acknowledging that it also drives diverse crises like increasing GHG emissions from transport infrastructure building and operation (14%, Lamb et al 2021), social conflicts, and the everyday iniquities of urban mobility, among others. Drawing on the interdisciplinary field of mobility studies, this course seeks to equip students to approach mobility as a complex phenomenon that has historically shaped landscapes and places, and poses many significant policy challenges. A specific aspect of the policy response to mobility challenges has been the creation of various mobility infrastructures - whether railways, freeways, air travel infrastructure, or light rail - which is conceived in the course as a mediating factor connecting policy and mobility realities including need, demand and experience. In this course, the interconnections between mobility, policy and infrastructure will be framed in the context of broader social concerns related to sustainability, equity and livability, culminating in a discussion of approaches and experiments leading to a sustainable mobility paradigm. The course content will include a mix of theory, case studies of policy `successes` and `failures,` especially from the Global South, and field visits/assignments. Modules: 1. Mobilities: How the socio-spatial world is constituted by a wide variety of more-than-human mobilities, their histories, interactions, policy responses to them, and the production of related infrastructures; conflicts and synergies between flows (of people, things and information) and places (villages, towns, cities); environmental impacts of accelerating mobility under globalisation. 2. Mobility actors and knowledges: Who moves, who enables movements, who makes policies, who pays for or profits from mobilities, and how do their knowledges of mobility vary? The differing value of and contradictions between these different knowledges; mechanisms for coordinating these knowledges in policy, planning and governance. 3. How India moves: mobility patterns across scales and urban/rural divides; mobility modes like for instance, migration, rural/urban commuting, mobility as way of life (pastoralism), ritual mobilities (walking pilgrimages) and their implications for policy and infrastructure. 4. Policy realities and orientations shaping mobilities in India: Institutional arrangements and orientations involved with contemporary mobility, policy and infrastructure in India. The policy, planning and governance challenges of responding to realities and challenges of mobility 5. Towards a sustainable mobility paradigm in urban policy: new technologies; ignored mobilities (walking, cycling) and their social and environmental significance; interactions between expert knowledge, policy and civil society

Description: Data science enables governments to optimize the allocation of public resources, evaluate the effectiveness of policies, and enhance service delivery across sectors such as health, education, and infrastructure. In addition to traditional econometric approaches, data science leverages advanced statistical and machine learning techniques to reach quicker and more precise results. Further, it facilitates cross-departmental insights, enabling departments to collaborate and share knowledge, leading to more holistic and impactful governance.Understanding the scope, methods, and applications of Data Science in Governance equips students of public policy with the means to analyse and manage large datasets, build models, track policy outcomes, generate actionable insights, and communicate these insights effectively. This course intends to bridge the gap between technical skills and policy analysis, fostering an understanding of the ethical and practical considerations involved in data use in governance, and ultimately supporting more responsive and inclusive governance practices. 1. Overview of data science and its role in policy analysis.a. How data science informs evidence-based policy makingb. Types of data: survey, administrative, open data.2. Basic concepts in statistics and probability. a. Descriptive and inferential statistics.b. Sampling and bias.c. Hypothesis testing.d. Discussion on observed biases in Indian socio-economic surveys and their implications3. Data collection, sorting, and cleaning.a. Digital Enterprise systems.b. Record Linkagec. Data wrangling: outliers, anomalies, missing data, deduplication.d. Ethics in data collection, storage, and use.e. Bias, fairness, transparency and interpretability, privacy.Case studies from Indian public databases- UIDAI, Aarogya Setu4. Building models.a. Regression models: DiD, RCT, IV, PSM, RDD etc.i. Discussed with reference to their application in relevant econometric papers.b. Spatial data.i. Nightlights and GDP datac. Supervised classification models.i. Policy targeting, etc.d. Unsupervised models: Clustering, biplots.i. Education/ Awareness studies5. Exploratory Data Analysis.a. Trends and patterns. Causation and correlation. 6. Data Communication. a. Principles of good data visualisation. b. Condensing and communicating insights from data analysis to a range of stakeholders.7. Historical records and NLP.8. Handling and analyzing big data. a. Cloud computing. b. Distributed data.

Description: This course provides a critical overview of the practice of urban planning, the historical underpinnings of its disciplinary knowledge, the urban challenges in the Indian context and planning`s responses. It provides a necessary framework to understand the institutional armature for all urban development and policy initiatives. The perspective of the course is critical and technical. It illuminates the explicit and tacit knowledge underlying the practice of urban planning in India. Through a key mapping exercise, (outlined in the practical component section below) students will understand how abstract policy instruments and tools capture reality, which then informs policy and planning.
